results.summary: Drug fever typically presents 7-10 days after drug initiation. Key features: relative bradycardia despite fever, eosinophilia, rash, and resolution within 48-72 hours of drug discontinuation. Unlike infection, drug fever patients often appear 'well' despite high temperatures.
results.title: Drug Fever: A Diagnostic Challenge for Internists

results.summary: Post-neurosurgical meningitis presents a unique diagnostic challenge. CSF pleocytosis may be attributed to surgery. Key distinguishing features: declining CSF glucose ratio (<0.4), elevated CSF lactate (>4 mmol/L), and clinical deterioration despite antibiotics suggest true infection. Partially treated meningitis may have atypical CSF profile.
results.title: Post-Neurosurgical Meningitis: Diagnostic Challenges

results.summary: Transient fever (up to 38.5°C) occurs in 5% of patients after EBP and typically resolves within 24 hours. Persistent fever >24 hours or fever >39°C should prompt evaluation for epidural abscess or meningitis.

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Administer the first dose of empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do NOT delay antibiotics for LP or imaging beyond what is strictly needed for safety.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue q6h for 4 days in confirmed pneumococcal meningitis.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain CT head before LP because imaging-first criteria are present (altered mental status, immunocompromise, focal signs, papilledema, or age >60).
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.
Reassess and de-escalate antibiotics based on Gram stain, culture, and susceptibility results.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Broaden empiric coverage to include staphylococci and gram-negative rods until cultures clarify; consult neurosurgery for CSF-leak repair planning.
Localise and repair the CSF leak after acute infection is controlled to prevent recurrence.

avoided_actions.rationale: No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotic timing matters: every hour of delay after the first hour increases mortality. Antibiotics MUST precede imaging or LP if either would delay treatment >60 minutes.
CT before LP is mandated when any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal signs, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60).
Adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h × 4 days) given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and unfavourable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans 2002, NEJM).
A negative CSF Gram stain (sensitivity ~60-90%, lower if antibiotic pretreated) does not exclude bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR or antigen testing retains sensitivity.
CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 is more reliable than absolute CSF glucose for distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis.
Empiric coverage must include vancomycin + ceftriaxone in adults; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage if age >50 or immunocompromised.
Post-neurosurgical or post-traumatic meningitis warrants broader empiric coverage (vancomycin + cefepime or meropenem) to cover staphylococci and gram-negative rods.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.

metadata.adaptation_notes: Source case was a 14-year-old diagnosed with drug fever post-EBP. This case inverts the diagnostic conclusion: the same clinical setup (post-neurosurgical patient with dural repair, CSF drain, EBP, rash, and fever) is used, but the underlying diagnosis is true bacterial meningitis that initially masquerades as drug fever. Age adjusted to 22 to meet schema constraints (18-90). Clinical complexity and red herrings from the source case are preserved and amplified.
metadata.difficulty_description: Initial presentation strongly mimics drug fever with concurrent rash, eosinophilia, and temporal relationship to medications and EBP. The key diagnostic evidence (elevated CSF lactate, worsening trajectory, positive cultures) requires follow-up investigations and careful clinical reasoning to distinguish from the more benign drug-fever interpretation.

patient.history_present_illness: A 22-year-old woman presents with fever, rash, and altered mental status in the neurosurgical step-down unit. She sustained frontal sinus fractures and a basilar skull fracture in a motor vehicle accident eight months ago, complicated by intermittent cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea. Ten days ago, she underwent surgical debridement and obliteration of the frontal sinuses with dural repair of an anterior cranial fossa defect. A lumbar CSF drain was placed intraoperatively and removed five days ago. During her perioperative course, she developed a pruritic maculopapular rash attributed to ceftriaxone, which resolved when antibiotics were changed to meropenem and vancomycin. After removal of the lumbar drain, she developed a severe positional headache with nausea, vomiting, and refusal to ambulate, consistent with post-dural puncture headache. Imaging at that time demonstrated a bifrontal extradural CSF collection. Three days ago, she received an epidural blood patch with 15 mL of autologous blood one interspace above the lumbar drain site, which significantly improved her orthostatic symptoms. Approximately 18 hours after the epidural blood patch, nursing noted that she was flushed and febrile to 38.8 degrees Celsius. She was no longer orthostatic and denied nausea or vomiting at that time. However, approximately 3 hours later she developed pruritus of the arms and legs with a fine maculopapular rash similar to her earlier ceftriaxone-related eruption. The primary team initially attributed the fever and rash to drug fever, potentially related to continued diphenhydramine or a delayed hypersensitivity reaction. Over the subsequent 12 hours, however, the patient has become increasingly somnolent with worsening headache that is no longer purely positional. She now reports photophobia and diffuse, constant headache rated 9 out of 10. The neurology service has been consulted for evaluation of possible meningitis versus drug fever versus epidural abscess complicating the recent blood patch.
